One Hundred Years of Solitude

by Gabriel Garcia Marquez · ★★★★★ · Finished sometime in 2025

One of my all time favourite books as of 2026.

What a beginning! And so much goes on! How realistic and fantastic at the same time. And what an ending. I loved this story.

If anyone asks me for a book recommendation, I will recommend this book to them. When I was buying Christmas gifts for my family after getting my first job, I decided to buy books for my siblings. I didn't care if they didn't like them. I bought a book for myself too, and it was this book. I saw that it won a nobel prize and after a quick internet search I decided to buy it.

I started reading it during my travel to and from my night shift job. While I sat in the well maintained public transportation system of Singapore, I was transported to a completely new universe inside this book. I love books or movies that start intensely, and this book starts something like this: When General Aureliano was going to be executed by gunfire, his whole life flashed before him and he remembered the first time his father showed him ice. And the story starts with a flashback and talks about the main family of the book.

Where do I start? I will do no justice to this story. But I could relate with most of the characters in this story. Even when some real surreal things started happening. Imagine a woman being raised straight to heaven after her death. Imagine a ranch with animals so fertile that its owner can keep cutting down cattle everyday and have a massive feast. Imagine the whole legacy of a family being wiped away by the wind, and hence the saying: gone with the wind.

What does this book not talk about? It talks about astronomy and alchemy, which is very interesting because even the Divine Comedy has references about these. I have not managed to understand all its implications, which would make a second or subsequent readings of the book even more rewarding. You have macho men in this book, but the women are more iconic and are way more important than the men. The men are all named Acardio or Aureliano or something like that. They keep making the same mistakes again and again and again. It gets so confusing, especially with their names being the same and everything. But for the women, lets talk about Ursula. She holds the whole family together with her immense willpower. She is the one place of activity and stability in that family. Someone equally iconic but opposite to her is Pilar Ternara, who probably had more than half of the children of the family. If anyone was more anti-patriarchy than her, I do not recall. And the best thing is that she probably does not even care about patriarchy.

Another aspect I would like to talk about is the impact of transnational capitalism on the land of Macondo (if I remember correctly) and the family. They are up to no good. I think Aureliano loses to them, but I do not remember. I distinctly remember the Americans coming and setting up banana plantations, exploiting the people of that region. And when the place was going to ruin, they packed up and left, looking for the next victim.

There were some hilarious moments too. There was the following quote:

“Bad luck doesn't have any chinks in it,” he said with deep bitterness. “I was born a son of a bitch and I'm going to die a son of a bitch.”
I remember laughing my head off while reading this in the MRT. I do not know how to explain it. It is just that I probably never expected these lines to be stated in the book, and also because of how true it is. It is so surreal, and that is quite how life is, isn't it? There are so many moments in the book where my eyebrows keep getting higher and higher. And I can't help but laugh in surprise.

One hundred years of solitude. It is about the growth of a family and the town associated with it. But this family as well as the town dies too, just like most things in life. 7 generations of the family. I better show you the family tree that is shown in the beginning of the book. It is impossible to understand this family tree. Why is everyone named Aureliano or Acardio? And why is the family so convoluted and why does one woman have kids with two different men of the family? This whole universe is very very different from the one I live in. But I can still relate with time.

The book ends with a bomb line, and that sentence was quite long. When I finished the book in the MRT, I was left in shock. The message I took out of that was that the families or people who keep making the same mistakes in this world do not get a second chance. Whenever the family was open and welcomed others, they did well. But when the family closed up, or when the members of the family closed up, they were all fated to doom. One hundred years of solitude would curse anyone to ruin.

At that time, I was in night shift, working from 8:30 pm to 9 am for half a week. From previous personal experience, whenever I would stay alone I would be absolutely miserable and waste my time on useless and mundane Youtube or Instagram reel sessions that would last upto 6 hours. Infact, the nights when I stayed at home and did nothing were the worst. After reading this book, I decided to commit my time and meet friends, preferably the same friends again and again so I could create a community or a strong social base. And that sparked my time in Public Mansion, one of the favorite eras of my life. Ofcourse, that is another story.

This book won a Nobel prize, and I see why. I would love to read it again, but for now I am busy with a lot of other shenanigans. Oh well. Until next time. (Sankalpa 29th October 2026)
